 She Misses Medicare’s Dec. 7 Deadline While Comparing Plans and Expects to Be Stuck for 2027. As a Medicare Advantage Member, She Gets One More Switch From Jan. 1 to March 31, a Second Chance Part D Members Miss
 By Gerelyn Terzo 
 Published November 18, 2026, 6:02am ET · 4 min read 
 The Full Benefits Desk desk. Editor: Gerelyn Terzo .
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 Medicare Advantage members who miss the Dec. 7 deadline get one plan change between Jan. 1 and March 31, but Original Medicare and standalone drug plan enrollees do not.
 Returning to Original Medicare risks steep out-of-pocket costs, since her Medigap guaranteed-issue window has closed and insurers in most states can deny her or charge more.
 Members should choose a replacement plan in December, secure Medigap approval before leaving Advantage, and use the special enrollment period if their plan is ending.

 An elderly woman intently reviews documents and books at her kitchen table, a common scenario for many seniors navigating the complexities of Medicare plan selection. This diligent process often precedes critical enrollment deadlines. © 24/7 Wall St. 
 A 72-year-old Medicare Advantage member spent November comparing 2027 plans side by side: drug lists, copays, and whether her heart specialist stays in network. She was still comparing when the Dec. 7 deadline passed. Now she assumes she is locked into a plan she never meant to keep. The Wall Street Journal’s recent profile of a couple who mastered open enrollment shows how much homework a good choice takes. For her, the deadline arrived before the homework was done.
 Because she is in an Advantage plan, she still has one move left. The Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period runs January 1 through March 31, 2027, and it is only open to people already enrolled in a Medicare Advantage plan, and you get one change. Enrollees in Original Medicare with a standalone Part D plan get no second chance. For them, the choice they made by Dec. 7 generally holds for all of 2027.
 One Switch, Two Directions, Zero Do-Overs
 The window allows exactly one of two moves:
 Switch to a different Advantage plan, with or without drug coverage.
 Leave Advantage, return to Original Medicare, and join a standalone Part D plan.
 It remains closed to Original Medicare enrollees who want to join Advantage, and to anyone hoping to trade one standalone drug plan for another. After she uses her one change, the next chance to fix a mistake comes in the fall 2027 enrollment period.
 Timing matters. New coverage starts the 1st of the following month after the plan receives the request. A request filed in early January means the new plan starts Feb. 1. A request filed on March 31 leaves her in the wrong plan for an entire quarter, paying its copays and filling prescriptions under its formulary.
 Returning to Original Medicare Carries a Price Most Members Miss
 Moving to another Advantage plan is the safe use of this window. Moving back to Original Medicare is where she can lose money. Using 2026 plan-year amounts from CMS, the Part B premium of $202.90 a month stays with her either way. Without a supplement, Original Medicare charges a $1,736 Part A deductible per benefit period and a $283 Part B deductible. After that, Part B coinsurance applies with no annual ceiling. If she is readmitted in a new benefit period, she owes the Part A deductible again. A hospital stay that runs past day 60 adds $434 a day.
 A Medigap policy closes that gap, but her one-time federal guaranteed-issue window closed six months after her Part B began. In most states, an insurance company can now review her health history and turn her down or charge her more. The Advantage window gives her no new Medigap protection. Two exceptions can rescue her. The first is a federal trial right, which applies if she joined Advantage for the first time within the past year. The second is living in a state with wider guaranteed issue, such as New York, Connecticut, Massachusetts or Maine.
 Here is the position: if she has a chronic condition, a recent hospital care or a cancer history, she should treat Original Medicare as off the table until a Medigap insurance company approves her in writing. A healthy member who passes underwriting can reasonably make the move, especially if her Advantage network has dropped specialists she depends on.
 Check Whether Your Plan Is Leaving Before You Switch
 Some Advantage plans are changing or ending for 2027. If her plan is ending and she does nothing, she returns to Original Medicare on Jan. 1, possibly without drug coverage. She would then no longer qualify for the Advantage window. An ended plan does come with its own protections, though. KFF says terminated Medicare Advantage members qualify for a special enrollment period for Medigap with guaranteed issue rights, which means she could buy a supplement without medical underwriting.
 Three Moves to Make Before Jan. 1
 Pick the replacement plan in December. Pull your plan’s 2027 Annual Notice of Change (ANOC) and enter your exact drug list, pharmacy and doctors into Medicare’s Plan Finder. Choose the plan now so you can file on Jan. 1 and have coverage start Feb. 1.
 Secure Medigap before leaving Advantage. If Original Medicare is your goal, apply for Plan G or Plan N first. Once you are approved, enroll in a standalone Part D plan during the window. That enrollment automatically ends your Advantage coverage, and you should set the Medigap start date to match.
 Read any nonrenewal letter carefully. If your plan is leaving, use the termination Special Enrollment Period and its guaranteed-issue Medigap right. That path costs nothing in screening, while the March 31 window offers no Medigap protection at all.
